# Every integer-centered symmetric common-vertex triangle chain satisfies OC

## Precise restricted theorem

Let m>=0. Let R=r_0>0 and let r_0,...,r_m>=0 satisfy

    R>=r_1>=...>=r_m,
    r_{h-1}-r_h <=r_h-r_{h+1}       (1<=h<m).

Put r_{-h}=r_h, T=conv(0,e1,e2), V=|T|=1/2, and

    S= union_{h=-m}^m {h} x r_h T,
    mu(A)=sum_{h=-m}^m area({x:(h,x) in A}),
    M=sum_{h=-m}^m r_h^2,
    y=(0,R/3,R/3).

Then y is a single deterministic point of S, and EVERY closed halfspace
H of the full ambient R^3 containing y satisfies

    mu(S intersect H) >= (2/9) V M.                 (T)

The constant is exactly 2^{-1}gamma_2, gamma_2=4/9. The number of
fibers is arbitrary. Oblique normals, zero normal components, repeated
radii, strict or non-strict concavity, and all closed boundaries are
included. Zero endpoint radii are permitted and treated exactly below. The theorem
is invariant under an integer translation or
reversal of the base and a common nonsingular continuous affine map
with a base-affine translation: (z,x)->(epsilon z+j,A x+b z+c),
epsilon=+/-1,j integer,det A!=0. Under such a map the displayed point
is sent to its actual image, all fiber areas multiply by |det A|,
and every original ambient closed halfspace is tracked bijectively.
Thus the theorem also covers a common nondegenerate triangle in place
of T with an affine common-vertex graph and an integer symmetry center.

For m>=1 the concave linear interpolation r(z) on[-m,m] gives the
actual full-dimensional convex body

    C={(z,x):-m<=z<=m,x1,x2>=0,x1+x2<=r(z)},

with exactly these integer fibers. Its peak fiber has positive area,
all fibers have dimension at most2, so q=2 and mu=H_2 on S. Finiteness and positivity are immediate from
0<V M<infinity and finite disjoint fibers. When m=0, the theorem is
simply an ordinary triangle statement; it also applies whenever one
such fiber is the only positive-area fiber of an ambient convex body.
Zero-area extra fibers add no H_2 mass and cannot invalidate(T).

This is a restricted theorem. It does NOT prove arbitrary nonsymmetric
radius chains, other continuous dimensions, general nonhomothetic
fibers, several integer variables, or OC in full. No intrinsic
lower-dimensional extension beyond its stated planar fibers is claimed.

## Proof of the theorem

Delete zero-area terminal fibers in symmetric pairs before the argument.
The positive radii remain a consecutive symmetric concave subsequence,
and the peak centroid and every closed cap mass are unchanged. The
measure remains H_2 because the peak has positive area. Thus this is an
exact deletion of zero measure, requiring no approximation or limiting
argument. Reuse m for the last positive radius.

Move the boundary of any containing halfspace parallel until it passes
through y; this can only reduce its mass. Apply dependency1. Every
original cap has a cap of no larger mass on each original fiber with
nonnegative nonzero continuous normal. Divide that normal by the sum
of its coefficients and exchange the continuous coordinates if needed.
It is now (a,1-a), 1/2<=a<=1, with ONE actual shared integer tilt beta.
The y coordinate remains the peak own centroid. Thus it suffices to
bound this normalized positive-normal cap for every real beta.

All formulas below use the dimensionless radius normalization R=1;
undoing it multiplies M and every cap area by R^2. It is a common
continuous scaling and leaves the integer coordinate fixed.

If m=0, ordinary planar Grünbaum gives cap>=4V/9>2V/9. For now
allow every m>=1; the one-pair low sector is proved directly below.

At a=1/2, dependency2 gives the stronger bound

    cap/V >=(2/9)M+1/243.

For a>=2/3 the paired-shift minimizers occur simultaneously at beta=0,
and the exact minimum is

    [a/(2a-1)]sum_h(r_h-1/(3a))_+^2.

Dependency3 bounds this below by f(a)M plus a positive finite remainder,
where

    f(a)=(3a-1)^3/[27a^2(2a-1)]>=1/4>2/9.

The derivative has sign3a-2 on this sector, establishing the stated
minimum at a=2/3. Therefore(T) holds throughout that sector.

Now suppose1/2<a<2/3. The one-pair case m=1 needs no prior
three-fiber theorem. Its exact pair floor satisfies

    Q_a(r)>=(8/3)(r-2/3)_+,       0<=r<=1.

Below2/3 this is nonnegativity. Between2/3 and rho=1/[3(1-a)],
the difference equals2(3ar-4a+1)^2/[9a(2a-1)]. From rho to1 the
difference is concave in r, is nonnegative at rho by that identity,
and at1 equals2(2a-1)/(9a). The peak own cap is at least1/2.
Thus for m=1 the cap deficit from its target is at least

    1/2+(8/3)(r-2/3)_+ -(2/9)(1+2r^2)>=13/162.

This expression decreases up to r=2/3 and increases thereafter,
with the displayed value at the join. This proves m=1 directly.
Hence assume m>=2 for the remainder.

Use the exact definitions of k_a,g,v,lambda,
c,rho,B,E(b),M0,M1,M2(b) in dependency4. That note proves directly
from the finite fiber tails that every shared-tilt cap satisfies

    cap/V >=g+sum_h k_a(r_h),
    cap/V >=g+v M,
    sum_h k_a(r_h)
       >=lambda[M-b^2-(1-b)^2/3]+k_a(b)-2B E(b),     (P)

where b=r_m and lambda>2/9. The first bound keeps the exact peak-fiber
surplus above its paired floor. The third retains the entire discrete
trapezoid error; original mixed mass is still M, not an integral.

Set alpha=(9+sqrt33)/24. For alpha<=a<2/3, v>=2/9 and g>0, so the
second inequality(P) proves(T). It remains that1/2<a<alpha.

Assume, for contradiction, that the original normalized cap is strictly
less than(2/9)M. Its own fiber gives M>M0. The second bound(P) gives
M>M1, since2/9-v>0 here. Independently, m>=2 and concavity give
r1>=(1+b)/2,r2>=b, so M>=M2(b). Combining the first and third bounds(P),
and using lambda-2/9>0, the purported cap deficit is at least

    g+(lambda-2/9)max(M0,M1,M2(b))
       +k_a(b)-lambda[b^2+(1-b)^2/3]-2B E(b).

Dependency5 proves this expression nonnegative on the entire remaining
a,b domain, by its explicit finite polynomial certificate. This
contradicts the strict cap deficit. Hence(T) holds also in this final
sector.

These cases exhaust all positive normals and every original shared
tilt. The initial domination therefore proves(T) for every original
closed ambient halfspace, including all oblique, mixed-sign, negative,
and vertical normal cases. Undoing the permitted continuous scaling
restores the factor R^2; the ratio constant is unchanged. The point is
the same actual peak own centroid throughout. This proves the theorem.
